lead: Wipers clear the screen with a small permanent-magnet motor that has two speeds and a park switch; a washer pump squirts fluid and the horn warns other road users. Keyless entry is a short radio conversation between a fob and the car, and the immobiliser is a second, stricter conversation that decides whether the engine may run at all. These are the body electrics a driver uses every day.

sections.h3: The wiper motor, its brushes and the park switch

blocks.text: A windscreen wiper motor is a permanent-magnet DC motor: two ferrite magnets give the field, and current reaches the armature through carbon brushes on a commutator. A worm gearbox cuts the motor's few thousand rev/min to roughly 40–70 wipes a minute, and a crank and link rods turn the rotation into the back-and-forth sweep of the arms.

Most wiper motors have three brushes. The common brush and the low-speed brush sit opposite each other. The high-speed brush is set closer to the common brush, so fewer armature conductors lie in series between the two brushes in use. Those fewer conductors generate less back emf at a given speed, so more current flows and the motor speeds up until the back emf balances the supply again. The supply stays 12 V; the speed changes only because a different brush is used.

The park switch is a cam-driven contact in the gearbox, not the stalk switch. When the driver switches off mid-sweep, the motor keeps running through the park contact, which the cam holds closed over most of the turn. At the park position the cam opens that contact and closes another that shorts the armature: the spinning motor acts as a generator into a short circuit, brakes hard, and the blades stop at the bottom of the screen.

The intermittent relay runs the motor for one wipe, waits, then repeats. In the simplest timer a capacitor charges through a resistor, and the relay fires when the capacitor voltage reaches about 63% of the supply. The delay is then one time constant:

blocks.where: T is the delay in seconds, R the timing resistance in ohms and C the capacitance in farads. A potentiometer on the stalk changes R so the driver chooses the delay; a body ECU does the same job with a software timer.

blocks.text: The washer system has a plastic reservoir, a small permanent-magnet motor driving a centrifugal pump that draws a few amperes, tubes with a non-return valve so the jets prime at once, and jets or fan nozzles aimed at the screen. A wipe-after-wash timer runs the blades two or three more strokes after the pump stops. Headlamp washers use a second, stronger pump. A rain sensor shines infrared light into the screen; dry glass reflects it back to a photodiode by total internal reflection, and water on the outside lets light escape, so the photodiode current falls and the wipers start.

An electric horn is a vibrating-diaphragm buzzer. Current through a coil pulls an iron armature fixed to a steel diaphragm; the movement opens a pair of contacts in series with the coil, the pull stops, the diaphragm springs back, the contacts close, and the cycle repeats a few hundred times a second. A tone disc on the diaphragm or a spiral trumpet (windtone horn) shapes the sound; an adjusting screw sets the contact gap and so the current and tone, and a capacitor or resistor across the contacts cuts arcing. Cars usually fit a high-note and a low-note horn together, switched by a horn relay so the horn button carries only the relay coil current.

sections.h3: Remote entry, passive entry and the immobiliser

blocks.text: Remote keyless entry (RKE) is a one-way radio link. A press of the fob sends a frame at 315 MHz or 433 MHz holding the fob's identity, the command (lock, unlock, boot) and a rolling code. The receiver in the body control module checks it and, if it is valid, drives the central-locking motors. Fob and receiver share a secret key and a counter; each press advances the fob's counter and sends a keyed code made from it. The receiver accepts codes a little ahead of its own counter, so presses out of range are tolerated, and rejects any old code, so a recorded press cannot be replayed.

Passive keyless entry removes the button: aerials in the door handles send a low-frequency wake-up at about 125 kHz, the fob answers on UHF, and the door unlocks when the handle is touched; with the fob inside, the start button works.

The immobiliser is a separate check. The key holds a transponder, a chip and a coil with no battery. A coil round the lock barrel or start button powers it at 125 kHz, sends a challenge, and the chip returns a response computed with its secret key. Only on a match does the immobiliser send a start enable to the engine ECU; without it the ECU will not fire the injectors or the coils, so the engine cranks but never runs.

examples.question: A wiper arm is 500 mm from pivot to tip and sweeps 120°. It makes 45 wipes a minute, one wipe being out and back. The intermittent timer uses 100 kΩ and 100 µF. Find (a) the average tip speed, (b) the peak tip speed if the arm moves like a crank-driven (sinusoidal) sweep, and (c) the intermittent delay.
steps: Sweep angle θ = 120 × π/180 = 2.094 rad; arc of one stroke s = rθ = 0.500 × 2.094 = 1.047 m; one wipe = 2 × 1.047 = 2.094 m.
Wipe rate = 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 wipes/s; average tip speed = 0.75 × 2.094 = 1.571 m/s.
In a sinusoidal sweep the speed is zero at each end and greatest mid-stroke, at π/2 = 1.571 times the average: 1.571 × 1.571 = 2.47 m/s.
examples.answer: (a) 1.57 m/s average; (b) about 2.47 m/s at mid-sweep, zero at the ends; (c) 10.0 s.

examples.question: Two horns each draw 4.5 A at 12 V. The horn relay coil has a resistance of 80 Ω. Find the current through the horn button with and without the relay, and the power the relay contacts switch.
steps: Without a relay the button carries both horns: 2 × 4.5 = 9.0 A.
With a relay the button carries only the coil current: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15 A.
Ratio 9.0 ÷ 0.15 = 60: the button current is cut 60 times.
Power switched by the relay contacts = 12 V × 9.0 A = 108 W.
examples.answer: 9.0 A through the button without a relay, 0.15 A with it; the relay contacts switch 108 W.

traps: High wiper speed comes from the third brush, which leaves fewer conductors and less back emf between the brushes in use; the supply stays 12 V.
The park switch is a cam contact in the gearbox, and it also brakes the motor by shorting the armature; examiners ask for both.
R × C gives seconds only with R in ohms and C in farads: 100 kΩ with 100 µF is 10 s, not 10 ms.
The immobiliser does not usually stop the starter. It withholds the start enable, so the engine cranks but the injectors and coils never fire.
Treating keyless entry and the immobiliser as one system. The fob's rolling code opens the doors; the transponder challenge and response allows the engine to start.

quiz.q: What does the park switch in a wiper motor do?
quiz.a: It keeps the motor running through a cam contact after the stalk is switched off, then opens at the park position and shorts the armature so the blades stop at the bottom of the screen.

quiz.q: Explain why a third brush gives a higher wiper speed.
quiz.a: The high-speed brush is set closer to the common brush, so fewer armature conductors are in series between the brushes. They make less back emf at a given speed, so more current flows and the motor speeds up until the back emf balances the 12 V supply again.

quiz.q: A wiper arm is 0.6 m long and sweeps 90° at 30 wipes a minute, one wipe being out and back. Find the average tip speed.
quiz.a: 90° = 1.571 rad; one stroke = 0.6 × 1.571 = 0.943 m; one wipe = 1.885 m; 0.5 wipes/s; average speed = 0.5 × 1.885 = 0.943 m/s.

quiz.q: An intermittent wiper timer uses 47 kΩ and 220 µF. Find the delay.
Explain how an electric horn keeps its diaphragm vibrating.
quiz.a: The coil pulls the armature and diaphragm, which opens contacts in series with the coil; the pull stops and the diaphragm springs back, closing the contacts again. This repeats a few hundred times a second, and the tone disc or trumpet turns the vibration into sound.

quiz.q: A car with the correct key cranks but does not start, and the immobiliser lamp flashes. Give two faults consistent with this and explain why.
quiz.a: The aerial coil round the lock barrel is open or its connector loose, so the transponder is never powered and never answers; or the immobiliser has lost its link to the engine ECU (a bus or wiring fault, or an ECU replaced without coding), so no start enable arrives. Either way the ECU withholds fuel and spark, so the engine cranks without firing.

quiz.q: How does passive keyless entry differ from remote keyless entry?
quiz.a: RKE needs a button press on a one-way UHF link. PKE has the car wake the fob with a low-frequency signal from the door-handle aerials; the fob replies on UHF and the door unlocks on touching the handle, and starting is allowed when the fob is inside.

quiz.q: Why is a rolling code safer than a fixed code?
quiz.a: A fixed code can be recorded and replayed. A rolling code is made from a counter that advances on every press, and the receiver rejects any code at or behind its own counter, so an old recording is useless.

beyond: Wiper and washer modules now sit on the LIN bus, so the body controller sends a speed or delay and the motor module does the rest. Phone-as-key systems use Bluetooth Low Energy and ultra-wideband ranging, which measures distance so a relay attack fails. Search terms: LIN wiper module, ultra-wideband digital key, transponder challenge-response.
